import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Convergence of the Flint Hills and Cookson Hills series

*References:*
- [Wikipedia: Examples of numerical series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Series_(mathematics)#Examples_of_numerical_series)
- [MathWorld: Flint Hills Series](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FlintHillsSeries.html)
- [Alekseyev, On the Flint Hills series](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1104.5100)
- [MathWorld: Cookson Hills Series](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/CooksonHillsSeries.html)
-/

namespace FlintCooksonHills

/--
The Flint Hills series summing $csc(n)^2 / n^3$ from $n=1$ to $\infty$ converges.
(Note that we 0-index the series below.)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 40]
theorem flint_hills_series_converges :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      Summable (fun n : ℕ =>
        1 / ((((n + 1) : ℝ)^3) * (Real.sin (n + 1)^2))) := by
  sorry

/--
The Cookson Hills series summing $sec(n)^2 / n^3$ from $n=1$ to $\infty$ converges.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 40]
theorem cookson_hills_series_converges :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      Summable (fun n : ℕ =>
        1 / ((((n + 1) : ℝ)^3) * (Real.cos (n + 1)^2))) := by
  sorry

end FlintCooksonHills

reformulations.difference: Uses unconditional `Summable` on a zero-indexed sequence instead of ordinary convergence of the series ∑_{m=1}∞ csc²(m)/m³.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Substituting m=n+1 gives exactly the source's summands: csc²(m)/m³ = 1/(m³ sin²(m)). All terms are nonnegative, so unconditional summability is equivalent to convergence of the ordinary partial sums to a finite real number. Review.flint_iff_source in /workspace/review/scratch.lean proves the equivalence with existence of a real limit of sums over Finset.Icc 1 N. The scratch file also proves that sine is nonzero at every positive integer, so totalized division introduces no exceptional terms.

reformulations.difference: Uses unconditional `Summable` on a zero-indexed sequence instead of ordinary convergence of the series ∑_{m=1}∞ sec²(m)/m³.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Substituting m=n+1 gives exactly the source's summands: sec²(m)/m³ = 1/(m³ cos²(m)). All terms are nonnegative, so unconditional summability is equivalent to convergence of the ordinary partial sums to a finite real number. Review.cookson_iff_source in /workspace/review/scratch.lean proves the equivalence with existence of a real limit of sums over Finset.Icc 1 N. The scratch file also proves that cosine is nonzero at every natural number, excluding exceptional division-by-zero values.

review.notes: Both declarations faithfully state the cited convergence questions. The answer placeholders have the correct proposition type and scope. The scratch file compiles successfully; its equivalence and nonvanishing proofs do not depend on sorryAx or the problem theorems. Boundary checks confirm that index 0 contributes the source's term at 1 and both denominators are always strictly positive. MathWorld still explicitly records both convergence questions as unknown, and Wikipedia does likewise for Flint Hills. I inspected the newer MathWorld-linked arXiv:2502.03474, which claims convergence, but the cited reference pages do not record it as an accepted solution; no confirmed status change is reported.
